items.prompt: What is 'trunk-based development', as defined in L1?
choices: A workflow where branches are extremely short-lived, merging back to a shared trunk frequently and continuously
A workflow where all developers commit directly to trunk with no branches at all, ever
A workflow that only applies to open-source projects with many external contributors
A workflow where trunk is renamed to 'main' as the only requirement
items.explanation: Trunk-based development is specifically characterized by short-lived branches merging frequently, not zero branches or a naming convention.
items.reference:
Trunk-based development
⏱️ Branches live hours to 1 day
🔁 Merges frequently and continuously
Why: short branch lifetime is what limits how much unreconciled overlap can build up.

items.prompt: According to L1, how long do branches typically live under trunk-based development?
choices: Often under a day
Several weeks
An entire quarter
L1 doesn't specify typical branch lifetime
items.explanation: L1 specifies branches often live under a day under trunk-based development — the defining property of the strategy.
items.reference:
Trunk-based development
⏱️ Branches live hours to 1 day
🔁 Merges frequently and continuously
Why: short branch lifetime is what limits how much unreconciled overlap can build up.

items.prompt: What is 'gitflow', as defined in L1?
choices: A workflow built around longer-lived branches that stay separate from trunk for an extended period before merging
A specific Git command for visualizing commit history
A rule requiring every commit to be reviewed by at least two people
A synonym for trunk-based development
items.explanation: Gitflow is specifically defined by longer-lived, separate branches — not a command, review policy, or synonym for trunk-based development.
items.reference:
Gitflow
⏱️ Branches live days to weeks
📦 Feature/release branches, separate from trunk
Why: real isolation, at the cost of a larger reconciliation later.

items.prompt: According to L1, how long do branches typically live under gitflow?
choices: Days to weeks
Under an hour
Exactly 24 hours, never more or less
L1 doesn't specify typical branch lifetime under gitflow
items.explanation: L1 specifies gitflow branches typically stay open for days to weeks, in contrast to trunk-based's under-a-day lifetime.
items.reference:
Gitflow
⏱️ Branches live days to weeks
📦 Feature/release branches, separate from trunk
Why: real isolation, at the cost of a larger reconciliation later.

items.prompt: What is 'branch divergence', as defined in L1?
choices: How much a branch and trunk have each independently changed since they last matched
The number of commits a branch has, regardless of trunk
A measure of how many developers are working on a single branch
The size in kilobytes of a branch's total diff
items.explanation: Branch divergence is specifically about independent change on both sides since the last common point — not raw commit count or file size alone.
items.reference:
Branch divergence
📈 Grows the longer a branch stays open
Why: divergence, not code volume, is what drives conflict cost.

items.prompt: According to L1, does branch divergence grow or shrink the longer a branch stays unmerged?
choices: Grows
Shrinks
Stays constant regardless of time
L1 doesn't address this relationship
items.explanation: L1 states divergence grows the longer a branch stays open — more time means more chances for both sides to independently touch the same files.
items.reference:
Branch divergence
📈 Grows the longer a branch stays open
Why: divergence, not code volume, is what drives conflict cost.

items.prompt: What is a 'feature flag', as defined in L1?
choices: A runtime toggle that lets incomplete or in-progress code merge to trunk safely, without being active for users yet
A code comment marking a section as needing review
A Git tag applied to a release commit
A warning issued by a linter for unused code
items.explanation: A feature flag is specifically a runtime toggle for safely merging unfinished work — not a comment, tag, or linter warning.
items.reference:
Feature flag
🚦 Runtime toggle
👤 Inactive for users until ready
Why: this is what makes frequent trunk merges practical for unfinished work.

items.prompt: According to L1, what makes frequent trunk merges practical even for work that isn't finished?
choices: Feature flags
Writing smaller commit messages
Disabling code review temporarily
L1 doesn't address how unfinished work gets merged safely
items.explanation: L1 identifies feature flags as the tool that makes merging unfinished work to trunk safe, since the code can stay inactive for users until ready.
items.reference:
Feature flag
🚦 Runtime toggle
👤 Inactive for users until ready
Why: this is what makes frequent trunk merges practical for unfinished work.

items.prompt: According to L1's scenario, how many conflicting files did Team Gitflow hit on merge day?
items.explanation: Team Gitflow hit 4 conflicting files on merge day after keeping their branch open the whole 10-day sprint.
items.reference:
The scenario
🌿 Gitflow: 4 conflicts, merge day
🌳 Trunk: 0 conflicts, whole sprint
Why: same file set, same sprint, different merge cadence.

items.prompt: According to L1's scenario, how many conflicts did Team Trunk hit across the entire 10-day sprint?
choices: Zero
items.explanation: Team Trunk, merging daily, hit zero conflicts across the entire sprint.
items.reference:
The scenario
🌿 Gitflow: 4 conflicts, merge day
🌳 Trunk: 0 conflicts, whole sprint

items.prompt: According to L2's flowchart, when does a conflict actually first exist — the moment it's created, or the moment it's discovered at merge time?
choices: The moment it's created — a long-lived branch delays discovery, it doesn't create the conflict by existing longer
Only at the moment of discovery, during the merge itself
Conflicts don't exist until a human manually flags them
L2's flowchart doesn't address when a conflict actually begins existing
items.explanation: L2 makes this point directly with its diagram's day-2 example — the conflict already exists once both sides touch the same file, well before any merge attempt discovers it.
items.reference:
Divergence accumulates
Day 1: trunk↔X, branch↔Y
Day 2: trunk↔Z, branch↔X — conflict exists NOW
Why: a long branch delays discovery, it doesn't create the conflict.

items.prompt: According to L2, what does a long-lived branch actually do to conflicts, if it doesn't create them by existing longer?
choices: Delays discovering conflicts that already happened, and lets more of them accumulate before discovery
Prevents conflicts from ever happening in the first place
Immediately resolves any conflict as soon as it occurs
Has no effect on conflicts whatsoever
items.explanation: L2 explicitly frames a long branch's effect as delaying discovery and allowing accumulation — not creating conflicts, and not preventing them either.
items.reference:
Divergence accumulates
Day 1: trunk↔X, branch↔Y
Day 2: trunk↔Z, branch↔X — conflict exists NOW
Why: a long branch delays discovery, it doesn't create the conflict.

items.prompt: According to L2's comparison table, what does trunk-based development require that gitflow doesn't?
choices: Feature flags, since code lands on trunk before it's fully done
A dedicated release manager for every merge
Weekly all-hands meetings to coordinate branches
A minimum team size of 10 engineers
items.explanation: L2's table specifically notes trunk-based requires feature flags for safely merging unfinished work, unlike gitflow's branch-based isolation.
items.reference:
The trade-off table
Trunk: small conflicts, needs flags
Gitflow: real isolation, bigger reconciliation
Why: neither column is correct in the abstract — it's a real trade.

items.prompt: According to L2, is gitflow's isolation ever genuinely useful, or is it strictly worse than trunk-based in every case?
choices: It's genuinely useful for work that shouldn't be visible on trunk yet, like a major rewrite or a security-sensitive change
Gitflow's isolation is never useful under any circumstances
Gitflow is only useful for teams of exactly one developer
L2 doesn't identify any case where gitflow's isolation helps
items.explanation: L2 explicitly identifies cases where real isolation genuinely helps — work that shouldn't be visible on trunk yet, like a major rewrite or security-sensitive change.
items.reference:
The trade-off table
Trunk: small conflicts, needs flags
Gitflow: real isolation, bigger reconciliation
Why: neither column is correct in the abstract — it's a real trade.

items.prompt: According to L2, why was Team Gitflow's integration so much harder, given both teams wrote roughly the same amount of code?
choices: The cost driver is unreconciled overlap accumulated over time, not code volume
Team Gitflow's engineers were less experienced than Team Trunk's
Team Gitflow used a different programming language
L2 doesn't explain why the two teams' experiences differed
items.explanation: L2 attributes the difference specifically to time spent unreconciled, not to code volume, skill, or tooling differences.
items.reference:
Time, not volume
⏱️ Overlap accumulates with time unreconciled
📏 Not proportional to code volume
Why: the strategy that resolves overlap sooner catches it smaller.

items.prompt: According to L2, can two developers write completely disjoint code for two weeks with zero conflict?
choices: Yes — conflict risk depends on overlap, not simply on how much time has passed or how much code was written
No — any two weeks of parallel work guarantees at least one conflict
No — disjoint code is impossible to write without coordination meetings
L2 doesn't address whether disjoint code avoids conflicts
items.explanation: L2 gives this exact example — disjoint code for two weeks can produce zero conflicts, while overlapping code for a single day can conflict immediately, showing overlap (not time or volume alone) is what matters.
items.reference:
Time, not volume
⏱️ Overlap accumulates with time unreconciled
📏 Not proportional to code volume
Why: the strategy that resolves overlap sooner catches it smaller.

items.prompt: According to L3, why does trunk-based simulation hit conflicts so rarely at 10 days?
choices: Each day's merge only ever risks that single day's overlap — a 1-in-6 chance per day of both sides touching the same file
Trunk-based development makes conflicts structurally impossible
The simulation was rigged to always produce zero conflicts
L3 doesn't explain why the conflict count was low
items.explanation: L3 attributes the low count to the small per-day overlap probability (1-in-6 with 6 hot files), not to conflicts being impossible.
items.reference:

10-day sprint, seed 42
0 conflicted merges
Why: each merge only risks that single day's overlap.

items.prompt: According to L3's verified gitflow simulation with the identical seed and 10-day file-touch sequence, how many conflicted files were found?

items.reference:

10-day sprint, same seed 42
4 conflicted files, one merge
Why: same underlying draws as trunk-based — only the check timing differs.

items.prompt: According to L3, what's different between the trunk-based and gitflow simulations, given they use the identical seed and file-touch sequence?
choices: Only when the overlap gets checked — daily for trunk-based, once at the end for gitflow
The gitflow simulation uses a completely different set of hot files
The gitflow simulation runs for a longer sprint than trunk-based
The two simulations don't actually share any underlying randomness
items.explanation: L3 states explicitly that both simulations use the same seed and underlying random draws — the only difference is the timing of when overlap is checked.
items.reference:

items.prompt: According to L3's extend-it results, what happens to gitflow's conflict count as the sprint length grows very long (e.g. 30 days)?
choices: It becomes bounded by the number of hot files (6) and stops growing much further
It grows without any limit, far exceeding trunk-based's count
It drops back down to zero regardless of sprint length
L3's extend-it section doesn't test sprint lengths beyond 10 days
items.explanation: L3 verifies gitflow's conflict count is bounded by hotFiles.length (6) since conflictedFiles can never exceed the total file count — confirmed at 30 days (6, same as 20 days).
items.reference:

5d: 0 vs 1 · 10d: 0 vs 4
20d: 2 vs 6 · 30d: 5 vs 6
Why: gitflow's count is bounded by file count; trunk-based's isn't.

items.prompt: According to L3, at 30 days, how do the two strategies' totals compare?
choices: Nearly equal — trunk-based reaches 5, gitflow reaches 6
Trunk-based is still exactly 0, unaffected by sprint length
Gitflow drops to 0, while trunk-based keeps rising
L3 doesn't test a 30-day sprint length
items.explanation: L3 verifies at 30 days trunk-based reaches 5 and gitflow reaches 6 — nearly equal, showing trunk-based's advantage isn't absolute but depends on realistic sprint lengths.

items.prompt: Implement `simulateTrunkBased(rand, days)`, matching L3: given `pickFile` and `hotFiles` are already available, for each of `days` days, independently pick a trunk file and a branch file; count how many days they matched (a conflicted merge). Return the total count.

tests.description: matches L3's verified seed-42, 10-day result of 0 conflicted merges
tests.expr: (() => { function mulberry32(seed) { return function () { seed |= 0; seed = (seed + 0x6d2b79f5) | 0; let t = Math.imul(seed ^ (seed >>> 15), 1 | seed); t = (t + Math.imul(t ^ (t >>> 7), 61 | t)) ^ t; return ((t ^ (t >>> 14)) >>> 0) / 4294967296; }; } const rand = mulberry32(42); return expect(simulateTrunkBased(rand, 10)).toBe(0); })()

(() => { function mulberry32(seed) { return function () { seed |= 0; seed = (seed + 0x6d2b79f5) | 0; let t = Math.imul(seed ^ (seed >>> 15), 1 | seed); t = (t + Math.imul(t ^ (t >>> 7), 61 | t)) ^ t; return ((t ^ (t >>> 14)) >>> 0) / 4294967296; }; } const rand = mulberry32(1); return expect(simulateTrunkBased(rand, 0)).toBe(0); })()

tests.description: conflicts every day when rand() always returns the same value (same file picked both sides)

items.explanation: This is the exact simulation L3 verifies at 0 conflicts for the seed-42, 10-day case — each day only ever risks that single day's overlap, which is why trunk-based's total stays low at realistic sprint lengths.

items.prompt: Implement `simulateGitflow(rand, days)`, matching L3: given `pickFile` and `hotFiles` are already available, accumulate the set of files touched by trunk and the set touched by the branch across all `days` days, then return the count of files present in both sets.

tests.description: matches L3's verified seed-42, 10-day result of 4 conflicted files
tests.expr: (() => { function mulberry32(seed) { return function () { seed |= 0; seed = (seed + 0x6d2b79f5) | 0; let t = Math.imul(seed ^ (seed >>> 15), 1 | seed); t = (t + Math.imul(t ^ (t >>> 7), 61 | t)) ^ t; return ((t ^ (t >>> 14)) >>> 0) / 4294967296; }; } const rand = mulberry32(42); return expect(simulateGitflow(rand, 10)).toBe(4); })()
